He was surprised to be asked about notice and non-compete in a first round.

candidate.subject: Fernhallow Capital first round: next steps
candidate.body:
Hi Oliver,

Thanks for talking me through your first round with Graham at Fernhallow Capital today.

Graham usually gets feedback back within two days. If we have not heard anything by Thursday, I will chase, and we will speak on Thursday. I will also go through the wording of your contract with you later, covering the notice period and non-compete.

For reference, the next round at Fernhallow is usually a technical at the office, with Python on real data plus a stats case, so it is worth getting some pandas practice in.

As I said, nothing about your search goes anywhere without your say-so.

Best wishes,
Hannah

client.subject: Oliver Brennan: Quantitative Researcher, Systematic Equities
client.body:
Hi,

Thank you for interviewing Oliver Brennan in the first round for the Quantitative Researcher, Systematic Equities role.

I would be grateful for your feedback when you have it, and I would be glad to hear your thoughts on next steps.

Best wishes,
Hannah

process.format: Video call of about forty-five minutes. About ten minutes on your CV, then probability questions typed into a shared document. No coding.
process.who: Graham Lowe, senior researcher. He gives little feedback during the call, mostly moving on with "OK, next one".
process.what_they_look_for: Accurate probability reasoning, checking your own answers, and how you validated past research (out of sample testing rather than tuning on the whole history).

process.format: Held at the office in two parts of about an hour each. Part one: a probability warm-up question, then live Python on a laptop provided by the firm with no internet access. Part two: a case discussion critiquing a backtest.
process.who: Nadia Osei, a researcher on the equities side, for the first hour. Nadia and another researcher, Pieter, for the case.
process.what_they_look_for: Sound logic over exact syntax, spotting problems in messy data before computing anything (such as survivorship bias), and finding the flaws in a backtest, including a detailed view of trading costs.

process.format: About three hours in total. A research presentation of a past project you can discuss without breaking confidentiality: thirty minutes to present, with presentation and questions together taking about an hour. Then thirty minutes with the head of research on culture and ways of working. It ended with a fifteen-minute one-to-one chat with the PM.
process.who: Marcus Elling (PM) and two researchers, Nadia and Felix, for the presentation. Ingrid Saarinen, head of research, for the culture conversation. Marcus for the closing chat.
process.what_they_look_for: Whether a signal is a known factor in disguise, an economic reason why it works and who is on the other side of the trade, and clear rules for when you would switch a live signal off. Marcus dislikes "the model found it" answers.

examples: Expected number of rolls of a fair die until you see a six
Expected number of coin flips until you get two heads in a row
The same question for heads followed by tails
Three random points on a circle: probability the triangle contains the centre
A stick broken at two random points: chance the three pieces make a triangle

question_themes.theme: Deep dive on past research and how it was validated
examples: How you handle crash periods in a momentum strategy, such as 2009
Whether the work was tested out of sample properly or tuned on the whole history

question_themes.theme: Live Python on messy equity data
examples: Using daily prices and volumes for a few hundred stocks over about ten years, with series that stop partway, gaps and bad prints, build a simple reversal signal and describe its performance
A backtest with a Sharpe ratio of about 2.1: "what's wrong with this"
How many variants do you think were tried to get this one
How would you model market impact for small caps, and at what participation rate
"Is this just value in disguise": have you neutralised against the standard factors
"What would make you kill this signal": what evidence and what threshold would make you switch it off live
How long would you wait: are you going to sit through six months of drawdown
Why does it work economically, and who is on the other side of the trade
How you deal with being wrong

went_well: On the two-heads-in-a-row question, giving four, then correcting to six and walking through the states, drew "good, you checked it" from Graham.
In the live Python, saying "I'd normally check the docs here" and writing the intended logic as pseudo-pandas drew Nadia saying that was fine and that she cares about the logic.
Asking, before computing anything, why some price series end (delisted or acquired), because dropping them introduces survivorship bias, drew a smile from Nadia.
When Marcus asked whether the signal was "just value in disguise", showing a backup slide with the factor-neutral version, where the effect drops but is still there, drew "OK, good".
Answering the kill-signal challenge by saying the position would be cut in size rather than killed outright, with the rule set before going live rather than after, drew a lot of nodding from Felix.
tripped_people_up: Describing out of sample testing as a holdout from 2019 onwards led Graham to ask who chose the holdout. The answer was the researcher who built the strategy.
In the backtest case, the interviewers pushed hard on costs, asking how to model market impact for small caps and what participation rate to assume, and the answer given was vague.
advice: For your second round, practise pandas work without internet access. If you cannot recall exact syntax, say so and write the logic clearly, as that is what Nadia assesses.
Before computing anything on the data set, look for series that stop, gaps and bad prints, and say how you would treat delisted or acquired names to avoid survivorship bias.

For the backtest case, work through look-ahead bias (such as trading at the same close used for the signal), costs and turnover, and multiple testing, including deflating the Sharpe ratio for the number of trials.
Prepare a concrete approach to market impact for small caps, including a participation rate you would assume, because costs drew more questioning than anything else in the case.
Expect a probability warm-up question at the start of the technical. Geometric probability questions on random points and broken sticks have come up.

For the final, bring backup slides showing your result neutralised against standard factors, an economic explanation of who is on the other side of the trade, and a kill rule set before going live, including how long you would sit through a drawdown.
The firm asks about notice and non-compete in every round, so be ready to state yours clearly: eight weeks' notice and a three-month non-compete.
logistics: Notice period and non-compete were asked about in the first round (by Graham, at the end), in the second round (by Nadia) and in the final (by Ingrid Saarinen).
Ingrid Saarinen stated that it is company policy not to buy out garden leave.
The live Python in the second round is done on a laptop the firm provides, with no internet access.
For the final presentation you may choose any past project you can discuss without breaking confidentiality. A sanitised version with no real numbers from a previous employer has been used.
Marcus asked for references at the final, before any offer.
Feedback after the second-round technical usually takes a few days.
